setup.label: Pawn to d4, on move three

beats.card: Open the centre on move three
beats.say: After e4 e5, a lot of openings spend several moves getting ready to play d4. The Scotch skips the preparation and plays it right now.
Think of it as knocking on the door instead of sending a letter first. Black has to answer on move three, before most of their pieces have left home.
It's not a trick, either. Kasparov brought it back to the top level against Karpov in 1990. And the same few ideas come up in nearly every line.
We'll build the setup, deal with the five ways Black tries to spoil it, learn the one punch, then watch it land in two games.
Four fixed moves, then three jobs in whatever order the position allows. Watch the list tick itself off.
Pawn to e4, and Black answers with e5. This walkthrough starts from there.
Knight to f3 attacks e5, and Black guards it. Everything's normal so far.
And here it is. Pawn to d4, on move three. That's a second hit on e5, and you didn't ask first.
Black usually takes. It's about three games in four among players under 1800 in our Lichess sample.
Your knight takes back, and it lands in the middle of the board.
Now count the centre. You have a pawn on e4, and Black has no centre pawn at all. That's what you came for.
Black hits the knight, so you trade it on c6. We'll come back to that. For now, notice Black's pawns: they're split up, and that lasts.
First job, the bishop. On d3 it guards e4. And the day that pawn moves on, the bishop's road opens straight to h7.
Second job. Castle, so your king's safe before anything gets sharp.
Third job. The other knight comes out and guards e4 again. That's the whole list.
Now look where your e-pawn wants to go: e5. In the London your pieces aim at that square. Here your pawn steps onto it. That push is the plan.
Your opponent didn't read the script. Here are the five things they'll try, and you only need one answer to each.
One. Black won't take, and holds e5 with the d-pawn instead.
Push straight past it. The knight has to move, and every square it can go to is worse.
It goes backward and blocks its own bishop. The engine says about plus 0.9, and you haven't given up a thing.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: Two, and the most common by far. About half the players under 1800 in our Lichess sample trade knights right here.
Queen takes, in the middle of the board. Normally that's asking to get chased. But the knight that would chase her just left.
So you simply develop, with the queen already in play. After the natural d6, the engine says about plus one.
Black's best idea is to offer a queen trade.
Step aside to c4. Black's queen left d8, so c7 has lost its guard, and your queen stays on the board.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: Three. Bishop to c5, and now your knight is attacked twice.
Trade it. That's your answer whenever this knight gets crowded. Most players take back with the b-pawn, which you saw in the setup. But watch the sharp try.
Black leaves your knight alone and threatens checkmate on f2.
Guard it with your queen, along the second rank. It looks clumsy, and it works.
Black takes back, and the engine calls it level. You've stepped around a mate threat, and that's all this one needed.
Knight to c3, then a4, chasing Black's best piece. Then bishop to d3 and castle, same as always.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: Four. The queen comes out early, and again your knight is hit twice.
Same answer. Trade it on c6.
Most players take back with the queen, and that hits your e-pawn.
Bishop to d3 guards it and does your first job at once. Black's queen is out in front of everything, and the engine says about plus 0.7.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Qf6 Nxc6
beats.say: And if they play bishop to c5 instead, look closely. It's reply three again, with the same threat on f2 and the same queen to d2.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: Five. It's rare, about one game in a hundred, but it's the one that steals a pawn. Queen to h4 goes straight for e4.
The knight guards it and develops.
But the bishop pins that knight to your king, so e4 isn't really guarded any more.
Here's the hard part. Let the pawn go. Bishop out, and you're ready to castle.
Black takes it. Now look at the black king, still at home, and at the pawn on c7, which has nothing guarding it.
Knight to b5. Next it lands on c7 and forks the king and the rook.
Black's best is to trade off that bishop first, then move the king to guard c7.
You castle. You're a pawn down, and the engine still likes White by about 0.7, because that black king won't be castling now.

chapters.title: The punch
chapters.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4

beats.say: Back to your knight on d4. One reply is left, and it's the one good players choose.
Knight to f6, hitting your e-pawn. It's natural development, and there's nothing wrong with it.
Trade first, same as always. Black's pawns get split up again.
Now the punch. The pawn Black just attacked steps forward and kicks the knight.
About six in ten players under 1800 in our sample jump to d5. It's the centre, so it feels right.
Kick it again.
Now look at it. Three moves spent on one knight, and it ends up on b6, at the edge of the action. The engine says about plus 0.4.
And that pawn keeps working. It takes f6 and d6 away from every black piece. Remember f6.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5
beats.say: A warning. This isn't a forced win. Black's best is queen to e7. Your pawn is pinned to your king, so it can't take the knight, and it's under attack.
Guard it with your queen on e2. Yes, it blocks your own bishop. That's the price.
The knight jumps, c4 kicks it, and the bishop hits back at c4. The engine calls this dead level. You haven't won anything. You've just asked a harder question.

beats.card: Game one: it goes to plan
beats.say: This game is made up by us and checked by Stockfish. Black's moves are all natural ones.

beats.play: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: The routine. Nothing to think about yet.
Knight to f6, and the trade.
Kick. Kick. You've seen this one.
Knight out, and Black hits it with the bishop.
Bishop to d3, already looking at h7. And Black castles straight into that.
You castle too, and Black takes on c3. Your pawns are a mess now. But look what Black gave away: the bishop that guards these dark squares.
Black starts chipping at your e5 pawn.
Your bishop comes out to guard it. And no black bishop can ever challenge this one now.
Now Black's knight and bishop both hit c4. That pawn's in real trouble.
You ignore it. Queen and bishop both hit h7, and that threatens mate. A big threat beats a small one.
Black blocks with g6, and it's safe for now. But look at the holes around that king.
So move in. Queen to h6, and she isn't leaving.
Here Black's best is to take on e5 and then push f6, and the engine says only about plus one. So far you've made no threat they can't meet.
But most people want their rooks connected. Queen to d7 looks tidy, and that's the mistake. It takes the engine from about plus one to above plus three.
Bishop to g5. Next stop f6, and then queen to g7 is mate.
And Black finally grabs that pawn. Pushing the f-pawn was the last real chance.
Bishop to f6. Nothing can take it, and nothing can guard g7.
Black takes your bishop too. It makes no difference.
Checkmate. Two mistakes, a tidy queen move and a free pawn. And the pawn that kicked the knight on move six held up the whole net.
Also ours, also engine-checked. This time Black plays the most common move of all.

beats.play: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: The routine again.
The knights come off, and your queen lands in the middle. Reply number two from the list.
Knight to f6, hitting e4. About one in five play this here, and it feels like ordinary development.
Your queen already guards e4. So punch. Same pawn, same square, and this time the engine is already at about plus two.
No good squares, so the knight goes all the way home. Black has spent two moves getting back to the start.
You just keep developing. You're miles ahead.
Black takes d5 away from your knight.
It was never going there. Knight to e4, and now look at d6. Your pawn guards that square, and so does your queen.
Black offers a queen trade, and that would be a good way out, if it gets the time.
It doesn't. Knight to d6 with check.
The only way to stay in the game is to take with the bishop, and lose that bishop for the knight. Then you're still well ahead, but there's a game left.
Instead the king steps up to e7. It keeps the bishop, but it also blocks it. Now nothing can touch that knight.
Your bishop arrives with check.
The king keeps walking. Pushing the f-pawn lasts longer, but that loses too.
Checkmate in the middle of the board, on move eleven. Black can't even block with d5, because your knight is standing on d6.

chapters.title: Your game plan
chapters.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4

beats.card: So how do you win with this?
beats.say: The opening is the easy part. Here's the whole plan in three lines.
One. d4 on move three, and the knight takes back. If that knight gets crowded, trade it on c6.
Two. When a knight lands on f6 and e5 is safe, push and kick it. A black pawn on d6 means it isn't safe yet.
Three. Keep that pawn alive, because it takes f6 and d6 from Black. Then bring everything towards the king: bishop to d3, queen to h5.
That's a good way to win quick games. It isn't a middlegame plan. A careful opponent plays queen to e7, it's level, and then you have to think.
So do two things next. Drill these lines until your hands know them, then read the Scotch plan for what to do when the punch doesn't land.
